about: Chemical Engineering Practice 1 (CENG40003) is the core, 10-credit practical module of Year 1 on Imperial's MEng Chemical Engineering, running across the Autumn and Spring terms (2026-27 programme specification). The specification describes the Foundation Lab and team-based design work; an older, undated department list groups a First Year Design Project, the Foundation Laboratory and an Introduction to MATLAB under CE1-03, which we infer corresponds to this module. Imperial does not publish a module-level syllabus or assessment breakdown, so this guide explains each component and how to prepare rather than setting out a syllabus.

notes.body:
Chemical Engineering Practice 1 (CENG40003) is the practical strand of Year 1 on Imperial's MEng Chemical Engineering. The programme specification lists it as a core module worth 10 credits, running across the Autumn and Spring terms.

What it contains
Imperial does not publish a single syllabus for CENG40003. An older, undated department page that uses the previous CE1- numbering lists three practical components under CE1-03:
- First Year Design Project
- Foundation Laboratory
- Introduction to MATLAB
We infer that CE1-03 is the forerunner of CENG40003 because the number and the practical content match, but no official page states this, and the current module may package things differently, so check the module's page on your learning platform and your timetable to see exactly which parts count towards it.

How it is assessed
The programme specification gives assessment only for Year 1 as a whole, not for this module: for a typical Year 1 pathway it shows 70% examinations, 20% coursework and 10% practical work across all Year 1 modules. That split does not tell you how CENG40003 itself is weighted. As the practical module, it is likely to be assessed through its lab, design and computing work rather than a single written exam, but that is an inference: confirm the exact components, weightings and deadlines in the module handbook.

How to approach it
- Treat every deliverable as assessed work: practical modules reward steady effort rather than last-minute revision.
- Keep a single organised record of lab sessions, design meetings and code.
- Use it to practise the theory from Process Analysis, Transfer Processes, Thermodynamics and Separation Processes: the lab and design work apply those ideas.

notes.h: The Foundation Laboratory: preparing, working safely and reporting
notes.body:
The programme specification describes the first-year Foundation Lab as teaching practical skills by illustrating relevant engineering scenarios. In practice that means running experiments on equipment linked to the theory you are learning, then analysing and reporting the results.

Before the session
- Read the lab script and the relevant lecture notes so you know what each measurement is for.
- Read the risk assessment and the COSHH information for any substances. Know where the emergency stops, eyewash and fire exits are.
- Plan a results table and the calculations you will do.

During the session
- Record raw data immediately, with units and an estimate of the uncertainty of each instrument. Do not tidy numbers before writing them down.
- Note conditions (temperature, flow settings, calibration details) and anything unexpected.
- Repeat readings where you can; repeats reveal random error.

Analysing results
- Distinguish random error (scatter, reduced by repetition) from systematic error (a consistent offset, such as a badly zeroed balance, which repetition does not remove).
- Propagate uncertainties. For a sum or difference, add absolute uncertainties in quadrature; for a product or quotient, add relative uncertainties in quadrature.
- Compare your results with theory or literature values and explain the difference quantitatively, not with vague "human error".
- Plot data so that the expected relationship is a straight line where possible, and use the gradient and intercept.

Writing the report
A typical technical report has: summary or abstract, introduction and aims, theory, method (brief), results, discussion (including errors), conclusions and references. Figures need numbered captions and labelled axes with units. Follow whatever template and length limit your demonstrators give you; that overrides any generic structure.

notes.h: The First Year Design Project: working as an engineering team
notes.body:
Design projects run through the Imperial Chemical Engineering degree. The programme specification describes design-based projects as team activities that require you to work effectively with other team members. The First Year Design Project is the first of these, and it introduces the habits that later, larger design projects build on.

What a design task usually involves
Specific briefs change from year to year, so use this as a general guide rather than a description of your project:
- Understanding the brief: what product or outcome is required, at what scale, and under what constraints (safety, cost, environment).
- Generating and comparing options, using clear criteria rather than gut feeling.
- Doing the engineering calculations to back up the chosen option, often including material and energy balances.
- Considering safety, sustainability and economics.
- Communicating the result in a report, presentation or poster.

Working in a team
- Agree roles, meeting times and internal deadlines early, and write them down.
- Keep shared files in one place with clear version names.
- Record decisions and who is responsible for each action after every meeting.
- Raise problems such as uneven workload with the team first, and with your supervisor early if they continue; do not wait until the deadline.
- Peer assessment is common in team projects at many universities, so contribute visibly; check your own project's rules on how individual marks are set.

How to do well
- Show your reasoning: state assumptions, justify choices and check calculations with an independent estimate.
- Present numbers with sensible significant figures and units.
- Proofread as a team: one consistent voice reads better than sections stitched together.

The older department list includes an Introduction to MATLAB within this practical strand, and the lab and design work both depend on careful engineering calculation. This note covers the computing and calculation habits you will use in every later module.

Calculation habits that save marks
- Always carry units through a calculation and check that both sides of an equation have the same dimensions.
- Convert to a consistent unit system (SI) before substituting numbers.
- Choose a basis (for example 100 mol of feed or 1 hour of operation) for material balance problems.
- The general balance for any quantity in a system is: input + generation − output − consumption = accumulation. At steady state accumulation is zero; for a non-reacting species generation and consumption are zero.
- Sanity-check answers: order of magnitude, sign and whether the result is physically possible (for example, a mole fraction above 1 means an error).

MATLAB essentials
- Arrays are indexed from 1, not 0.
- * is matrix multiplication; .* , ./ and .^ act element by element. Using * when you meant .* is one of the most common errors.
- Ending a line with a semicolon suppresses printed output.
- Write scripts and functions rather than typing into the command window, comment your code and give variables meaningful names.
- Built-in tools useful in chemical engineering include solving linear systems (A\b), finding roots of equations (fzero), integrating ordinary differential equations (ode45) and plotting results with labelled axes.

How to prepare
- Practise little and often. Re-do worked examples without looking, then change the numbers.
- Use MATLAB to check hand calculations from other modules, for example solving a set of linear material-balance equations.

cards.b: 10 credits, core, running across the Autumn and Spring terms of Year 1 (programme specification).
Programme-level only: about 70% examination, 20% coursework, 10% practical across Year 1 for a typical pathway. No per-module split is published.
Random error scatters readings and is reduced by repetition; systematic error shifts all readings the same way and is not removed by repeating.
Accuracy: closeness to the true value. Precision: closeness of repeated measurements to each other.

cards.f: Uncertainty in a product or quotient
cards.b: Add relative uncertainties in quadrature: δq/q = √((δx/x)² + (δy/y)²) for independent random errors.

cards.f: Uncertainty in a sum or difference
cards.b: Add absolute uncertainties in quadrature: δq = √(δx² + δy²) for independent random errors.
Hazard: something with the potential to cause harm. Risk: the likelihood that harm occurs combined with its severity.
Elimination, substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls, then personal protective equipment as the last resort.
The Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations 2002 (Great Britain): require assessment and control of exposure to hazardous substances.
* is matrix multiplication; .* multiplies arrays element by element (similarly ./ and .^).
Starts at 1: x(1) is the first element.

questions.q: A sample's mass is 25.00 ± 0.02 g and its volume 10.0 ± 0.1 cm³ (independent random errors). What is its density with uncertainty?
questions.why: ρ = 25.00/10.0 = 2.500 g/cm³. Relative uncertainties are 0.02/25.00 = 0.08% and 0.1/10.0 = 1%; combined in quadrature ≈ 1.0%, so δρ ≈ 0.025, quoted as ±0.03 g/cm³. ±0.12 g/cm³ comes from adding the two absolute uncertainties (0.02 + 0.1) even though they are in different units from each other and from density. ±0.0008 is the mass's relative uncertainty (0.02/25.00) quoted as if it were an absolute uncertainty in density, and it ignores the much larger volume uncertainty. 2.5000 ± 0.1 quotes too many significant figures and simply reuses the volume's absolute uncertainty.

questions.q: A balance that was not zeroed adds 0.15 g to every reading. What type of error is this?
questions.why: A constant offset that affects every reading in the same way is a systematic error; repeating the measurement will not reveal or remove it. Random error causes scatter in both directions. Parallax applies to reading scales by eye, not to a digital zero offset. Rounding error comes from limited displayed digits, not a fixed offset.

questions.q: In MATLAB, x = [1 2 3] and y = [4 5 6]. Which expression returns [4 10 18]?
questions.why: x.*y multiplies corresponding elements: 1×4, 2×5, 3×6 = [4 10 18]. x*y attempts matrix multiplication of two 1×3 row vectors, which gives a dimension error. x*y' is the dot product, a single number (32). x(0) is invalid because MATLAB indexing starts at 1.

questions.q: Before a Foundation Laboratory session using a heated vessel and a dilute acid, what preparation should you do, and how would you apply the hierarchy of control to the hazards?
markScheme: Read the lab script, theory and risk assessment/COSHH information beforehand
Identify hazards: hot surfaces/steam and corrosive or irritant acid
Apply hierarchy: eliminate or substitute (lower temperature or concentration), engineering controls (guards, fume cupboard, splash screens), administrative (procedures, supervision)
PPE (goggles, lab coat, gloves) as the last line of defence; know emergency equipment locations
questions.modelAnswer: Before the session I would read the lab script and relevant theory, plan my results table, and read the risk assessment and COSHH information for the acid. The main hazards are burns from hot surfaces or steam and skin or eye contact with the acid. Following the hierarchy of control: first ask whether the hazard can be eliminated or reduced by substitution, for example by using the lowest acid concentration or temperature that still meets the aims. Next use engineering controls, such as guarding hot surfaces, using splash screens or a fume cupboard and secure clamping. Then administrative controls: following the written procedure, working under supervision and never leaving heating unattended. Finally, wear PPE (safety glasses or goggles, lab coat and gloves) and know where the eyewash, emergency stop and spill kit are.
